# Thursday links: MCPs and debt stories

[Blockworks has an MCP](https://blockworks.com/insights/introducing-the-blockworks-mcp-our-data-your-agents)

One way to understand the significance of the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is to think about it as a progression of who can do what on the internet.

First, the HTTP standard enabled humans to visually browse the web: Open Weather.com, for example, and see tomorrow’s forecast.

Later, APIs allowed software to access the web: The app on your phone can ask Weather.com for tomorrow’s forecast.

Now, the MCP standard allows LLMs to act on the web: “Hey agent: Check tomorrow’s forecast and if it’s sunny, send an email to my manager saying I’m not feeling well.”

You, hard-working reader, would never do that, of course. But you might want your agent to check some crypto prices?

If so, you could do that yourself by checking a website, thanks to HTTP. Or open an app on your phone that queries a database, thanks to APIs.

As of recently, though, you can also ask an LLM.

You probably won’t, though, because LLMs tend to hallucinate about things like that — unless they’re connected to a reliable source of data. This is what MCP is for.

First developed by Anthropic in November 2024, the [Model Context Protocol](https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol) is a set of rules (hence “protocol”) that standardize how LLMs connect to external tools and sources of data.

In the case of onchain data, you might ask Claude what the price of bitcoin has been doing lately. Claude can then query Blockworks’ MCP server (if you’re a [subscriber](https://blockworks.com/products/data)), where it will see a menu of all the data Blockworks provides. Seeing that market data on bitcoin is of course available, Claude then requests recent prices. Blockworks delivers the data to Claude and Claude delivers it to you.

In whatever form you requested it.

Launch OpenClaw & Hermes Agent Instantly Claude Helped Researchers Break Into OpenAI Three researchers reached employee accounts and internal repositories in less than 72 hours Hacktron researchers combined flaws in OpenAI’s community forum and login system to take over employee accounts. With Claude’s help, they demonstrated access to internal repositories without reading the code, then reported their findings. Key Points: New Model, Different Result: Opus 4.8 struggled to build a working exploit, but Opus 5 succeeded within hours of its release. Codex Proved the Breach: The team used an employee’s Codex account to submit a harmless proposed change to OpenAI’s private code repository. Fixed and Rewarded: OpenAI confirmed its fix roughly 14 hours after the report and paid $6,500 for the OpenAI vulnerability, not the forum attack.
